messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark Daniels was 52, a married school principal in a large North American city, and until recently he had prided himself on being the steady adult in every room. The assault happened on a winter evening after a late parent conference, when he stepped into the nearly empty parking lot behind the school and a stranger came up fast from between the cars. It lasted only minutes, but the details had fixed themselves in him with unnerving clarity: the hard edge of a forearm across his chest, the shove that sent him sideways against the cold metal of a sedan, the flash of the man’s hand near his waistband that made Mark think a weapon might appear. Since then, when he tried to deliberately remember what happened, the memory would not come in on command; it felt blocked, as if his mind kept a gate half closed. Yet the experience was not gone. It returned in fragments that played over and over like a film he could not stop—an angle of pavement, the sound of his own breath, the sensation of his body pinned in the same twisted position as if it were happening again. Those involuntary scenes carried a charge that made the world feel unsafe in the present tense. Mark found himself jumpy at ordinary noises and, almost before he knew he was doing it, scanning for exits as soon as he entered any room or building. He also noticed potential weapons and dangerous objects everywhere: the umbrella stand in the office lobby, the heavy trophy on a shelf in the teachers’ lounge, the metal paperweight on his desk. Even in places he had always regarded as familiar, his attention kept catching on what could be used against him.

Over the following weeks, the memory intrusions shaped the way he moved through his days. Mark was still going to work, but he began arriving early so he could check the building before students and staff filled the halls. He took longer routes through the school and positioned himself near doors, telling himself it was just efficient administration, though what he was really doing was making sure he knew how to get out. The parking lot at dismissal became especially difficult, because the open space and the rows of vehicles resembled the place where he had been attacked, and once he saw a man hurry toward his truck with a toolbox in hand he felt his body jerk before he could stop it. That reaction embarrassed him, but it also confirmed what he had come to believe: if he relaxed for even a moment, something like the assault could happen again. So he kept scanning, not only for exits but for anything that could become a threat, and the more he monitored his surroundings the more dangerous the world seemed to feel. At home, his wife noticed that he sat facing the door during dinner and flinched when a pan clattered in the kitchen. Mark did not tell her how often the memory replayed in his head; instead he gave short answers, tired of trying to explain something he could not fully summon on purpose anyway. What frightened him most was not simply the assault itself, but the way the memory could still seize his body and pull him back into that helpless posture without warning, leaving him convinced that danger was always one step away. 

By the time he sought help, the strain was no longer something he could manage by sheer discipline. He had become exhausted from watching every doorway, every parking lot, every object that might be used as a weapon, and he was worried that the children and staff were starting to notice how tightly wound he had become. He came to treatment after nearly stepping out of a faculty meeting because a maintenance cart had been left near the exit and he could not stop thinking about how quickly it could block his escape. Mark said he wanted to feel like himself again, to stop living as if every building concealed an attack, and he was most afraid that if the replayed memory and constant alertness kept tightening around him, he would eventually become the kind of man his wife already saw—present on the outside, but always braced for the next blow.
